week.weeklyOverview: Toddlers practice noticing big feelings at school—happy, sad, mad, scared, and calm—through mirrors, short stories, puppets, and repeatable calm-down games. Each day offers one clear feeling focus with simple words, large washable materials, and process-first art (no perfect crafts). Teachers model naming feelings, gentle helping, and quick reset strategies so toddlers build security with classmates and caregivers.
week.weeklyMaterials:
Emotion picture cards (happy, sad, mad, scared, calm)
Child-safe handheld mirrors
Soft puppets and stuffed animals
Feelings chart at toddler height
Washable crayons, markers, and paint
Large paper / construction paper
Glue sticks and yarn scraps (optional)
Scarves and bean bags
Feathers or pinwheels for breathing practice
Calm-down bottles (securely sealed; no loose beads for mouthing)
Play dough
Music player for freeze/dance transitions
Smocks, wipes, and a quiet calm corner mat
week.teacherPreparation: Prep one tray at a time at toddler height. Keep Back to School materials chunky, washable, and mouthing-safe.
week.familyConnection: Each evening, ask “What feeling visited you at school today?” Offer two choices if needed (“happy or tired?”). Practice one calm strategy together—three feather breaths or a cozy hug count. Celebrate any feeling talk; naming emotions at home helps toddlers use the same words with teachers and friends.
milestones: Language: Uses or approximates feeling words (happy, sad, mad, calm) with gesture or picture support
SEL: Notices a peer’s feeling and tries a kind action with teacher coaching
Motor: Imitates simple face motions, dance freezes, and fine-motor process art marks
Cognition: Matches a face card to a feeling word and recalls one calm-down choice

printableIdeas.title: School Feelings Picture Card Pack
printableIdeas.purpose: Large happy/sad/mad/scared/calm cards for chart work, matching, freeze dance cues, and calm-corner visuals.

printableIdeas.title: Calm Choice Cards
printableIdeas.purpose: Picture choices (breathe, hug a teddy, ask a teacher, drink water) used after Helping the Mad Monster and Pinwheel Breathing.

songs.title: Feelings Face Chant
songs.motions: Show each face on cue; gentle cheek wipe motion for sad; two soft stomps then hands on heart for mad/rest; hands on belly for breathe.
songs.teacherDirections: Hold matching emotion cards while chanting. Invite toddlers to copy faces in mirrors. Keep stomps soft and brief; move quickly into calm breathing.
songs.whenToUse: Morning circle with the Feelings Chart; before Feelings Match-Up
songs.transitionPurpose: Preview today’s feeling vocabulary and settle into circle
songs.lyrics:
Happy face, happy face, smile so wide,
Sad face, sad face, tears we can dry.
Mad face, mad face, stomp then rest,
Calm face, calm face—breathe is best.

songs.title: Breathe In, Blow Soft
songs.motions: Hands on belly for breathe in; soft blow toward a feather/pinwheel; shoulders drop; hands rest in lap on better.
songs.teacherDirections: Use during Calm Breathing with Feathers or Pinwheel Breathing. Model one breath at a time. Offer a quiet alternative (hand on heart) if blowing is hard.
songs.whenToUse: After big energy, conflict coaching, or before rest
songs.transitionPurpose: Reset bodies and voices toward calm
songs.lyrics:
Breathe in slow, breathe out soft,
Shoulders down, hands aloft.
Breathe in slow, blow a feather,
Calm comes back—we feel better.

songs.title: If You're Happy and You Know It
songs.motions: Clap; for mad verse one soft stomp then hands on heart; for calm verse belly breaths—avoid long stomping chains.
songs.teacherDirections: Keep verses short. Prefer original Feelings Face Chant for deeper emotion practice; use this traditional song for joyful participation only. Do not invent copyrighted pop song variants.
songs.whenToUse: Happy Dance Party or outdoor Happy Walk warm-up
songs.lyrics:
If you're happy and you know it, clap your hands.
If you're happy and you know it, clap your hands.
If you're happy and you know it, then your face will surely show it.
If you're happy and you know it, clap your hands.

(Additional verses teachers may use: If you're mad… stomp once then rest. If you're calm… breathe in slow.)

books.title: The Color Monster
books.author: Anna Llenas
books.whyThisBook: Colors mapped to feelings give toddlers a concrete way to sort and name emotions at school.
beforeReadingQuestions: What color feels happy to you today?
duringReadingPrompts: Which feeling is the monster showing on this page?
afterReadingQuestions: What feeling might you put in a jar today?
books.substituteTitle: Use emotion color cards and Feelings Face Chant if the book is unavailable.

books.title: Glad Monster, Sad Monster
books.author: Ed Emberley & Anne Miranda
books.whyThisBook: Flip-style monster faces make happy/sad talk playful and easy to imitate with mirrors.
beforeReadingQuestions: Can you make a glad face in the mirror?
duringReadingPrompts: Is this monster glad or sad?
afterReadingQuestions: Tell a friend one thing that makes you glad at school.
books.substituteTitle: Mirror, Mirror, Happy Me with glad/sad cards.

books.title: Llama Llama Misses Mama
books.author: Anna Dewdney
books.whyThisBook: Separation feelings are familiar for toddlers starting or returning to school; the story normalizes missing and reconnecting.
beforeReadingQuestions: Have you ever missed someone at school?
duringReadingPrompts: How does Llama Llama feel right now?
afterReadingQuestions: What helps you feel brave when you miss someone?
books.substituteTitle: Helping Teddy Feel Brave with a short teacher story about missing and reuniting.

books.title: Today I Feel Silly
books.author: Jamie Lee Curtis
books.whyThisBook: Many feelings in one story expand vocabulary beyond happy/sad for curious toddlers.
beforeReadingQuestions: What feeling word do you want to listen for?
duringReadingPrompts: Show me that feeling with your face.
afterReadingQuestions: Which feeling from the book did you notice today?
books.substituteTitle: Optional enrichment title—if time is short, keep the top three books; use feeling cards for a mini walk.

books.title: Grumpy Monkey
books.author: Suzanne Lang
books.whyThisBook: Validates mad/grumpy days and models that friends can still care without forcing fake smiles.
beforeReadingQuestions: Is it okay to feel grumpy sometimes?
duringReadingPrompts: What does Jim Panzee need from friends?
afterReadingQuestions: What helps you when you feel grumpy at school?
books.substituteTitle: Optional fifth title—enrich fully only if schedule allows; otherwise note for family lending library.

teacherToolkit.teacherPreparation: Prep one tray at a time at toddler height. Keep Back to School materials chunky, washable, and mouthing-safe.
prepChecklist: Set materials at child height before arrival
Preview one Back to School invitation aloud
Place cleanup caddy near the play space
Review allergy and supervision notes for the day
observationFocus: Uses Back to School vocabulary in play
Persists with a material or peer exchange
Shows interest or curiosity during invitations
observationPrompts: What language or gestures appear during play?
How does the child enter and leave the invitation?
Where do peers support or extend the idea?
documentationPrompts: Capture one moment of child-led exploration (with permission).
Note a verbatim quote or gesture tied to the theme.
teacherTips: Model once, then narrate what you notice.
Offer two choices instead of open-ended demands.
Keep transitions short with a familiar song cue.
setupCleanupShortcuts: Trays labeled and stacked by day
Damp cloth + bin for quick reset
Spare substitution basket on the shelf

materialSubstitutions.use: printed picture cards or recycled clean containers

teacherToolkit.mixedAgeAdaptations: Younger toddlers explore with larger pieces; older peers get a second sorting rule or helper job.
teacherToolkit.extraSupportAdaptations: Sit beside, shorten the invitation, and offer hand-under-hand only when welcomed.
teacherToolkit.challengeExtensions: Invite children to invent a new Back to School rule, map, or story for peers.
teacherToolkit.safetyInclusionNotes: Use child-safe mirrors and securely sealed calm bottles—no loose water beads or small parts that toddlers might mouth. Washable, large materials preferred. Art is process-based with smocks and wipeable surfaces. Supervise breathing props; provide non-mouthing alternatives. Keep emotional coaching inclusive: all feelings are welcome, and no child is forced to perform a feeling face for photos.
teacherToolkit.endOfWeekReflection: Which Back to School words and strategies showed up most in play?
teacherToolkit.familyConnection: Share one Back to School word or song to try at home during ordinary routines.
teacherToolkit.notes: Draft toolkit for owner review — enrichment draft only.

legacySnapshot.weeklyOverview: My Feelings at School helps toddlers recognize, name, and express their emotions in healthy ways while adjusting to the school environment. Throughout the week, children will explore feelings such as happy, sad, excited, frustrated, scared, and calm through stories, dramatic play, art, music, and hands-on activities. They will practice identifying emotions in themselves and others, learn simple calming strategies, and build empathy, kindness, and confidence as they develop positive relationships with teachers and classmates.
legacySnapshot.objectives:
Identify and name common emotions.
Express feelings using words, facial expressions, and actions.
Develop empathy for classmates.
Learn simple calming strategies.
Build confidence and emotional security at school.
Strengthen communication skills.
Practice problem-solving during social situations.
Build positive friendships and classroom relationships.
